subject: CREATIVE ARTS
title: Indigenous Kenyan Games (Optional)
overview: Indigenous animal games are optional games in which players copy the way animals move. Kenyan children have played versions of these games for a long time, with little or no equipment. You will name several animal games, perform them safely, and then fit the movements to a musical beat. You will also see how the games build fitness and health.

lessons.title: What indigenous animal games are
objectives: Explain what makes a game an indigenous animal game.
Name animals that Kenyan children copy in play.
Give one reason these games support health.
lessons.intro: Watch a goat skip, a frog leave the ground, or a hen spread her wings, and you already have the idea of an animal game. The game is the animal’s movement turned into play with rules.
lessons.notes:
An indigenous game is a game that communities pass on through play. It is not bought in a box. Children learn it from other children, from elders, or from a teacher who is keeping that play alive. An animal game uses the movement of an animal as the main action.

Kenyan children copy animals they know: the frog by the stream, the rabbit, the duck, the crab, the snake, the elephant, the hen and the hawk. You do not need a special pitch. A clear compound is enough. That is one reason these games are indigenous activities. They grew out of local play, local animals and local spaces.

### What you will be able to name
- **Frog jump:** a deep squat and a two-footed jump.
- **Rabbit hop:** hands and feet on the ground, hopping forward.
- **Duck walk:** a walk in a deep squat with the hands on the hips or behind the back.
- **Crab walk:** belly up, moving on hands and feet.
- **Elephant walk:** a heavy forward bend, one arm swinging like a trunk.
- **Snake crawl:** a low crawl on the tummy.
- **Hen and hawk:** a chasing game in which a hen guards chicks from a hawk.

These names describe the movement. Different communities may use their own language for the same kind of play. Ask what the game is called where you live, and add that name. Do not invent a name and pretend it is traditional.

Even one of these games makes the heart beat faster and the legs work. Playing them often is a way of building fitness without expensive equipment. That health role is as important as the fun.

keyWords.meaning: a game passed on through community play
a game whose main movement copies an animal

examples.problem: A class buys a video game about animals and plays it sitting down. Is that an indigenous animal game?
steps: Indigenous animal games are active play passed on in the community.
They copy animal movement with the body.
examples.answer: No. An indigenous animal game is physical play that copies an animal, learnt through community play.

examples.problem: Why might the same frog game have two names?
steps: Different communities speak different languages.
The movement can be the same.
examples.answer: Communities may name the game in their own language.

activity.title: Name the animal and the movement
materials: Pictures or a short video of animals and of children playing animal games
steps: Watch a live demonstration or a video of two animal games.
Write the animal, the movement you saw, and any skill such as jumping, crawling or chasing.
Add a name used in your own community if you know it for certain.
Tell a partner one way the game could make the body fitter.
Agree a clear space where the class can play next time.

practice.question: What is an indigenous animal game?
practice.answer: A game passed on through community play in which the main movement copies an animal.

practice.question: Name three animal games.
practice.answer: Any three: frog jump, rabbit hop, duck walk, crab walk, elephant walk, snake crawl, hen and hawk.

practice.question: Give one reason animal games help health.
practice.answer: They make the body work, for example by jumping, crawling or chasing, so they build fitness.

summary: Indigenous animal games copy animals and are passed on through play.
They need little equipment and a clear space.
They are enjoyable and they build fitness.

lessons.title: Frog jump, rabbit hop and duck walk
objectives: Perform a frog jump, a rabbit hop and a duck walk.
Keep a safe distance from other players.
Count a set of jumps accurately.
lessons.intro: Three small animals give three different leg skills. The frog leaves the ground, the rabbit travels on hands and feet, and the duck stays low and walks.
lessons.notes:
Warm up with a slow jog and by circling the ankles and knees. These games bend the knees deeply. Cold knees are more easily hurt.

### Frog jump
Squat with the feet a little apart and the hands on the floor between the feet. Look forward. Push with the legs and jump forward, landing on both feet with the knees bent. Stand up between jumps if you need to. Count ten jumps, rest, and count ten more. 10 + 10 = 20 jumps. Counting keeps the game fair and links it to mathematics.

### Rabbit hop
Squat and place both hands on the ground ahead of you. Hop the feet toward the hands, then walk the hands forward again. The movement is hands, then feet. Keep the head up so you can see other players. Hop for a short distance, then rest.

### Duck walk
Sink into a squat and walk forward without standing. Hands can rest on the hips. Keep the heels down if you can. Take ten steps, stand and shake the legs, then take ten more.

### Safety
- Play in one direction so nobody jumps into a friend.
- Leave a gap you could stretch your arms into.
- Land softly. Hard landings on the heels jar the back.
- Stop if a knee hurts and tell the teacher.
- The ground should be flat and free of stones and sticks.

A good performance is controlled, not the wildest. You should be able to stop on a signal without crashing.

keyWords.meaning: a two-footed jump from a squat, like a frog
a hop that travels by moving the hands forward and then the feet
walking forward while staying in a squat

examples.problem: A learner does 10 frog jumps, rests, and does 10 more. How many jumps is that?
Two groups frog-jump toward each other. What is the safer arrangement?
steps: Players should move in one direction.
A gap prevents collisions.
examples.answer: All players should jump in the same direction with space between them.

activity.title: Three animal travels
materials: A start line and a finish line a short distance apart
steps: Warm up the knees and ankles.
Frog-jump from the start line, counting ten landings, then rest.
Rabbit-hop the same distance with a gap between players.
Duck-walk ten steps and stand.
On a signal, freeze. Tell a partner which animal movement you controlled best.

practice.question: How does a frog jump land?
practice.answer: On both feet, with the knees bent.

practice.question: What is the order of a rabbit hop?
practice.answer: Hands forward, then feet hop toward the hands.

practice.question: Why leave a gap between players?
practice.answer: So that nobody jumps or walks into another person.

summary: Frog jump: two feet, soft landing.
Rabbit hop: hands then feet.
Duck walk: stay low, then stand and rest.

lessons.title: Crab, elephant and snake
objectives: Perform a crab walk, an elephant walk and a snake crawl.
Change from one animal to another on a signal.
Protect the wrists, back and knees.
lessons.intro: The frog used the legs. The next three animals share the work with the arms and the back. Control matters more than speed.
lessons.notes:
### Crab walk
Sit, hands behind you, fingers pointing to the feet if that feels comfortable for the wrists. Lift the hips and walk on the hands and feet, belly facing up. This is a moving cousin of the crab balance, but here the hips travel. Keep the hips up. Move slowly. If the wrists hurt, stop and shake them.

### Elephant walk
Bend forward from the hips with a long back, not a collapsed one. Clasp the hands to make a trunk, or let one arm swing. Take heavy, slow steps. An elephant game is not a race. The control is in staying bent and moving together.

### Snake crawl
Lie on the tummy and pull yourself forward with the forearms, legs trailing, head up enough to see. Do not crawl over anyone. A snake stays low. If the ground is rough, crawl on grass or a mat, not on gravel.

### Changing animals
The teacher calls “frog”, “crab”, “elephant” or “snake”. Change as soon as you hear the word. This trains listening as well as the body. Freeze when you hear “herd stop”.

### Safety and roles
One learner can be the caller. That is a real role, not a punishment. Another can watch for collisions. Players who are resting should stand outside the space. Rotate so everyone plays and everyone serves.

These movements strengthen arms, stomach and legs in different ways. The crab and the snake work the upper body. The elephant challenges the back and the legs to stay controlled. Quality is a straight path and a clean stop.

keyWords.meaning: moving on hands and feet with the belly facing up
a slow walk bent forward, with an arm as a trunk
a low crawl on the tummy

examples.problem: A learner’s wrists hurt in the crab walk. What should they do?
steps: Pain is a stop signal.
They should not keep walking on sore wrists.
examples.answer: Stop, shake the wrists, and tell the teacher.

examples.problem: Why is the snake crawl unsuitable on gravel?
steps: The body is on the ground.
Gravel can cut the skin.
examples.answer: The tummy and arms would be cut or scratched. Use grass or a mat.

activity.title: Change the animal
materials: Clear flat ground or mats for crawling
steps: Practise the crab walk, the elephant walk and the snake crawl separately.
On the caller’s animal name, change movement.
Freeze on “herd stop”.
Swap the caller.
Name one body part that worked hard in each animal.

practice.question: Which way does the belly face in a crab walk?
practice.answer: Up.

practice.question: What signal should make every player stop?
practice.answer: The agreed stop signal, such as “herd stop”.

practice.question: Name one safety rule for the snake crawl.
practice.answer: Crawl on grass or a mat, not on gravel, and do not crawl over other people.

summary: Crab: belly up, hips lifted, move slowly.
Elephant: long back, slow steps. Snake: low crawl on a smooth surface.
Change on a call and freeze on the stop signal.

lessons.title: Hen and hawk
objectives: Play a hen-and-hawk chasing game with clear roles.
Use a safe tag instead of grabbing clothes or hair.
Explain the animals the game copies.
lessons.intro: Not every animal game is a race in a straight line. Some are chasing games. Hen and hawk copies a bird protecting her chicks from a hunter in the sky.
lessons.notes:
Hen and hawk is a chasing game played by children in many Kenyan communities. The animals are the hen, the chicks and the hawk. You may know it by another name at home. Use the local name if you know it, and keep the safety rules the same.

### Roles
- One player is the **hen**. The hen guards the chicks.
- Several players are the **chicks**. They form a line behind the hen, each holding lightly at the waist of the person in front. The hold is gentle. Do not clutch clothing around the neck.
- One player is the **hawk**. The hawk tries to tag the last chick.
- The hen spreads both arms and moves from side to side to block the hawk. The line of chicks moves with the hen.

### Rules
- The hawk must not push through the line or grab hair.
- A tag is a light touch on the arm or back of the last chick, not a shove.
- If the hawk tags the last chick fairly, that chick becomes the hawk and the hawk joins the line as a chick. Rotate the hen as well so one person is not always at the front.
- Play inside a marked space so the line does not run into a wall or a road.
- If the line breaks, stop and join up again.

### What the game trains
The hen and chicks change direction together. That is agility. The hawk dodges. Everyone must watch. The game also needs unity: if one chick lets go or pulls the wrong way, the line fails. Taking turns with the hard roles is part of responsibility.

Stop on the whistle even if a tag is about to happen. Safety outranks the point.

keyWords.meaning: a chasing game in which a hen guards a line of chicks from a hawk
a light touch that counts as a catch
the ability to change direction quickly and safely

examples.problem: There is 1 hen, 1 hawk and 8 chicks. How many players are in the game?
The hawk grabs a chick by the hair. Is that a fair tag?
steps: A tag is a light touch on the arm or back.
Grabbing hair is unsafe.
examples.answer: No. The tag does not count, and the hawk must use a light touch.

activity.title: Play hen and hawk
materials: A marked open space away from roads
steps: Choose a hen, a hawk and a line of chicks. Hold waists gently.
Play until a fair tag or until the whistle blows.
Rotate the hawk and the hen.
Rest, then play once more with a new line.
Discuss how the hen’s spread arms are like a real hen protecting chicks.

practice.question: What are the three roles in hen and hawk?
practice.answer: Hen, chicks and hawk.

practice.question: How should chicks hold on?
practice.answer: Lightly at the waist of the person in front, never around the neck.

practice.question: What happens after a fair tag in the version in this lesson?
practice.answer: The tagged chick becomes the hawk and the hawk joins the line.

summary: The hen guards a line of chicks from the hawk.
A tag is a light touch, not a grab.
Rotate roles and stop on the whistle.

lessons.title: Safety, space and fair roles
objectives: Set up a safe playing area for animal games.
Follow and help enforce the stop signal.
Take more than one role in a game.
lessons.intro: A fast hawk and a strong frog jump are only good skills if the players go home unhurt. Safety is a part of performing the games, not an extra lecture after the fun.
lessons.notes:
Before any animal game, set the space.

### The ground
Pick flat ground. Remove stones, sticks, bottles and tins. If you are crawling, choose grass or mats. Keep away from roads, open drains, beehives and tied animals. A game that copies a goat should not be played beside a real, nervous animal.

### The body
Wear clothes you can bend in, and shoes that fit, or play barefoot only on ground the teacher has checked. Tie hair. Empty pockets. Warm up the ankles, knees and wrists.

### The rules that prevent injury
- Move in the direction the leader gives.
- Keep a gap.
- Land softly from jumps.
- Tag lightly. No hair pulling, no neck holds, no tripping.
- The whistle or the words “herd stop” mean freeze at once.
- Rest before you are exhausted. Breathless, dizzy or in pain means stop and tell the teacher.
- One group plays while another watches. A crowded space causes crashes.

### Roles
Players, caller, hawk, hen, and a lookout who watches for danger at the edge of the space are all roles. Sharing them is fair and teaches responsibility. The lookout is playing the game too, because without a lookout the game is not safe.

Animal games improve fitness only when you can play them again tomorrow. An injury ends the fitness. Obeying the rules is how you keep the health benefit.

keyWords.meaning: a player who watches the edge of the space for danger
a whistle or a call that means everyone freezes

examples.problem: The best open ground is beside a busy road. Should the class play there?
steps: A safe space is part of the game.
A road is a danger even if the ground is flat.
examples.answer: No. Choose a clear space away from the road.

examples.problem: A class of 30 all frog-jump in a small courtyard at once. What is a safer plan?
steps: Crowding causes crashes.
Groups can take turns.
examples.answer: One smaller group jumps while the others watch, call or rest, then they swap.

activity.title: Set the space, then play
materials: A compound the teacher has approved
Markers for the corners of the space
steps: Walk the space and remove loose hazards.
Mark the corners and choose a lookout.
Warm up, then play one animal game in groups that take turns.
Practise freezing on the stop signal three times.
Rotate so each learner has been a player and has held another role.

practice.question: Give three safety checks before animal games.
practice.answer: Any three: clear the ground, keep away from roads, warm up, tie hair, leave a gap, agree a stop signal, play in turns.

practice.question: What does the lookout do?
practice.answer: Watches the edge of the space for danger.

practice.question: Why do safety rules protect the health benefit of the games?
practice.answer: An injury stops you playing. Safe play lets you keep building fitness.

summary: Clear the ground and stay away from roads and drains.
Leave gaps, tag gently and freeze on the signal.
Share roles, including caller and lookout.

lessons.title: Animal games on a musical beat
objectives: Move as an animal in time with a steady beat.
Use clapping, a drum or another percussion instrument.
Stop and start with the music.
lessons.intro: A frog that jumps whenever it feels like it is only half the game. When the jump sits on a drumbeat, the whole group becomes one herd.
lessons.notes:
Indigenous animal games become even more enjoyable when they join a musical rhythm. The beat can come from handclaps, a drum, a shaker, or another percussion instrument the class already knows.

### Making the beat
The caller claps a slow steady pulse: clap, clap, clap, clap. Count “1, 2, 3, 4” aloud. Then a drum takes the same pulse. The beat must be slow enough for a duck walk or a crab walk. A beat that is too fast forces people to crash.

### Fitting the animal to the beat
- **Frog:** jump on beat 1, land and rest on beats 2, 3 and 4. Then jump again.
- **Rabbit:** hands on beat 1, feet on beat 2, and repeat.
- **Elephant:** one step on each beat, slow and heavy.
- **Duck:** one step on each beat, staying low.
- **Snake:** pull forward on beat 1 only, rest on the other beats.

Start and stop with the drum. When the drum stops, the animals freeze, even if a jump has begun. That control is part of the performance.

### Performing for others
One group plays instruments. One group moves. Then they swap, so the musicians also get the fitness and the movers learn to keep a beat. A short performance might be 16 beats of frog jumps. Counting 4 groups of 4 beats gives 16. If the class can keep those 16 beats together, the rhythm is working.

The music does not replace safety. The lookout still watches, and the space stays clear. Enjoy the sound and the movement, but do not add a beat so loud that the stop signal cannot be heard.

keyWords.meaning: a repeated pattern of beats
the steady beat you can count
instruments played by hitting or shaking

examples.problem: Frog jumps happen on beat 1 only. In 4 counts, how many jumps does one player make?
steps: Only beat 1 is a jump.
There is 1 jump in each group of 4 counts.

examples.problem: Four groups of 4 beats make how many beats?

activity.title: Move with the drum
steps: Clap a slow 1-2-3-4 count.
Practise frog jumps on beat 1 only.
Change to elephant steps on every beat when the caller changes the animal.
Swap so players become the musicians.
Perform 16 beats and freeze when the sound stops.

practice.question: On which beat does the frog jump in this lesson?
practice.answer: Beat 1, then the player rests on beats 2, 3 and 4.

practice.question: Why must the beat be slow for a crab walk or a duck walk?
practice.answer: A fast beat makes players rush and crash.

practice.question: What do the animals do when the drum stops?
practice.answer: They freeze at once.

summary: Use a slow, steady beat from claps or a percussion instrument.
Match each animal to a simple count.
Start and freeze with the music, and swap roles.

lessons.title: Fitness and health from animal games
objectives: Match each animal game to a part of fitness.
Explain how regular play supports a healthy life.
Plan a short practice that is hard enough but safe.
lessons.intro: Fun is the reason children keep playing. The fitness happens inside the fun. If you can name what the body is gaining, you can value the games for health and not only for a noisy afternoon.
lessons.notes:
Different animals build different kinds of fitness.

- **Frog jumps** strengthen the legs and train you to land with control. The heart and lungs work harder when you do a set of jumps.
- **Rabbit hops and crab walks** strengthen the arms, shoulders and stomach.
- **Duck walks** challenge the leg muscles to keep working while you stay low.
- **Snake crawls** strengthen the arms and the middle of the body.
- **Elephant walks** practise control and posture.
- **Hen and hawk** trains agility, speed and the ability to watch other people.
- **Playing on a beat** adds coordination, because the body and the sound must agree.

Health is wider than strong legs. These games are played with other people, so they practise unity and responsibility. They can be played after school without buying equipment. They also teach you to notice real animals: how a frog pushes, how a hen guards chicks, how an elephant steps. That habit of looking supports what you learn about animals in Agriculture.

A healthy plan for one session:
1. Warm up.
2. Two animal travels, with counts.
3. A short hen-and-hawk game or a rhythm performance.
4. A stretch and a drink of water.

Playing every day until you are in pain is not healthy. Playing often, stopping on the signal, and resting when you are dizzy is how the games serve a healthy lifestyle. Value the games because they make you able, not because they let you show off.

keyWords.meaning: the strength, stamina and control to do physical tasks well
moving the body in time with a plan or a beat
the ability to keep going

examples.problem: Which game is the better match for arm strength: a duck walk or a snake crawl?
steps: The duck walk works the legs in a squat.
The snake crawl pulls with the arms.

examples.problem: A learner plays hen and hawk until they feel dizzy, then continues. Is that a healthy choice?
steps: Dizziness is a stop signal.
Health includes rest.
examples.answer: No. They should stop, tell the teacher and rest.

activity.title: Name the fitness
steps: In groups, match each animal game you know to one fitness benefit.
Perform a short circuit: 8 frog jumps, a rabbit hop across a small gap, and 8 duck steps.
Add 16 beats of one animal if a drum is available.
Stretch and drink water.
Write one reason you value animal games for health.

practice.question: Which body parts do frog jumps strengthen most?
practice.answer: The legs, and they also make the heart and lungs work.

practice.question: What does hen and hawk train besides speed?
practice.answer: Agility, watching others, and working together.

practice.question: Why is playing until you are dizzy not healthy?
practice.answer: Dizziness is a warning. Rest keeps the game safe and lets you play again.

summary: Each animal movement builds a different part of fitness.
The games also teach teamwork and need no expensive kit.
Warm up, play, stretch, and stop if you feel unwell.

lessons.title: A class animal-games performance
objectives: Perform two animal games, one of them to a beat.
Carry out a role for the class performance.
Appreciate the games as fitness and as community play.
lessons.intro: A performance collects what you have learnt: the animals, the safety, the beat and the reason the games are worth keeping. The audience should be able to name the animal and see the control.
lessons.notes:
Plan a short display of about three parts.

1. **Travel.** The class, in two turns, performs frog jumps and then elephant walks across a clear space. The lookout watches the edges.
2. **Rhythm.** A percussion group plays 16 slow beats. Movers do one animal on the beat, then freeze when the sound stops.
3. **Chase.** One small group plays hen and hawk with light tags, while the others sit outside the space and keep still.

Every learner has a role: mover, musician, hen, chick, hawk, caller or lookout. Rotate if you have time so that nobody only watches. The caller explains the local name of any game the class knows for certain, and the animal it copies.

The audience does not run into the space. They clap after each part, not during a jump, so the performers can hear the beat and the stop signal.

Afterwards, answer two questions. How did these games make the body work? Why do they count as indigenous activities? Your answers should mention community play, local animals, little equipment, and fitness. Pride in the performance should include pride in playing safely. A display in which someone is pushed or laughed at has missed the point of the games.

You can play these games at break, in a club, or at a class games time, as long as the space is safe and an adult knows what you are doing.

keyWords.meaning: a prepared performance for an audience
the people watching

examples.problem: A performance has 16 beats of movement and the frog jumps only on every first beat of a 4-beat group. How many frog jumps is that?
steps: 16 ÷ 4 = 4 groups.
One jump in each group.

examples.problem: The audience runs alongside the hawk to get a better view. What should they do instead?
steps: The audience stays outside the space.
Running in makes the game unsafe.
examples.answer: Sit or stand outside the marked space and clap after the part has finished.

activity.title: Perform the three parts
steps: Set the space and agree roles.
Perform the travels, then the rhythm section, then a short hen-and-hawk game.
The audience stays outside and claps at the end of each part.
Rotate one role if time allows.
Discuss fitness and why the games are indigenous, then stretch.

practice.question: Name the three parts of the display.
practice.answer: Animal travels, movement on a beat, and hen and hawk.

practice.question: Give two reasons animal games are indigenous activities.
practice.answer: Any two: they are passed on through community play, they copy local animals, they need little equipment, they use local spaces, communities have their own names for them.

practice.question: Where does the audience stand?
practice.answer: Outside the marked space.

summary: Perform travels, a rhythm section and a chasing game.
Everyone has a role, and the audience stays clear.
Value the games for fitness, fun and community play.

quiz.question: An indigenous animal game is…
options: community play that copies how an animal moves
quiz.explanation: The games are passed on through play and use animal movements.

quiz.question: Which movement is a frog jump?
options: Walking on the hands with the belly up
A two-footed jump from a squat
A line of chicks holding waists
A slow bend with an arm as a trunk
quiz.explanation: The frog jumps from a squat and lands on both feet.

quiz.question: In a rabbit hop, what moves first?
quiz.explanation: The hands go forward, then the feet hop toward them.

quiz.question: During a crab walk, which way does the belly face?
quiz.explanation: The crab walk travels on hands and feet with the belly up.

quiz.question: A fair tag in hen and hawk is…
options: a light touch on the arm or back
quiz.explanation: The tag must be gentle and must not grab hair or the neck.

quiz.question: 10 frog jumps plus 10 frog jumps equals…
When the drum stops, the players should…
quiz.explanation: The stop in the music is a stop in the movement.

quiz.question: Why should the beat be slow for a duck walk?
quiz.answer: A fast beat makes players rush and bump into each other.
quiz.explanation: The rhythm must fit the movement and the safety of the space.

quiz.question: Snake crawls especially strengthen…
options: the arms and the middle of the body
quiz.explanation: Pulling the body along the ground works the arms and the core.

quiz.question: Give one reason to value animal games for health.
quiz.answer: Any one: they strengthen muscles, raise the heart rate, build agility, need no expensive equipment, or can be played often and safely.
quiz.explanation: The games are a practical way to keep fit.
